narrative:
The model predicted a 66.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the middle of their class. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; your fourth-decile placement falls well below the sixth-decile average of accepted applicants.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 36, your score is only slightly below the 37.18 average of accepted students, so it provided a modest pull toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10, family income in the upper-middle bracket, and plan to attend full-time were less influential and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most affected this prediction. (218 words)
